extraction.name: POPE: Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation for Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
extraction.description: POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation) is a benchmark dataset and evaluation framework for assessing object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). It converts hallucination evaluation into a binary classification task by prompting LVLMs with Yes/No questions about objects in images. The dataset includes three sampling strategies (Random, Popular, Adversarial) and is built on MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA datasets. It evaluates whether LVLMs generate objects inconsistent with ground-truth image content.
extraction.creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen (Renmin University of China, Meituan Group)
extraction.citeAs: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen. Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv:2305.10355v3, 2023.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The evaluation dataset is constructed from the validation set of MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA datasets. For MSCOCO-based POPE, 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects are randomly selected, and 6 questions are constructed per image. Ground-truth objects are obtained either from human annotations or from automatic segmentation using SEEM. Negative (nonexistent) objects are sampled using three strategies: Random, Popular, and Adversarial sampling.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images and object annotations from MSCOCO validation set (2,000 images randomly sampled for CHAIR evaluation; 500 images for POPE evaluation), A-OKVQA, and GQA datasets. Object segmentation results are also obtained using the SEEM automatic segmentation tool.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Three negative object sampling strategies are applied: (1) Random Sampling: randomly sample objects not present in the image; (2) Popular Sampling: select the top-k most frequent objects in the whole dataset that do not exist in the current image; (3) Adversarial Sampling: rank objects by co-occurrence frequency with ground-truth objects and select top-k frequent ones not present in the image. The ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects is set to 1:1 for label balance.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For CHAIR evaluation, 2,000 images are randomly sampled from the MSCOCO validation set. Only 80 objects appearing in the MSCOCO segmentation challenge are considered. For POPE, 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects are selected. Six questions are constructed per image (l=6), with equal numbers of positive (ground-truth) and negative (nonexistent) object questions. For SEEM-based POPE, automatic segmentation is applied to annotate images from MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Ground-truth object labels are derived from existing human annotations in MSCOCO. For unannotated datasets (A-OKVQA, GQA), the SEEM automatic segmentation tool is used to generate object annotations. Polling questions are formulated using the template 'Is there a/an <object> in the image?' with answers being 'Yes' or 'No'.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) automatic segmentation tool for unannotated datasets; existing MSCOCO human annotations for annotated settings.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The consistency between POPE Yes/No responses and model-generated captions was analyzed. Out of 1303 and 1445 objects given 'No' responses by InstructBLIP and MiniGPT-4 respectively, merely 0 and 5 were referenced in captions. Out of 664 and 1034 objects mentioned in captions, 664 and 961 received 'Yes' verdicts, confirming strong correlation. Performance gap between annotation-based and SEEM-based POPE was noted (e.g., F1 Score 71.37 vs. 62.70 for MiniGPT-4 under Adversarial setting), attributed to finer granularity of SEEM segmentation.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) for automatic object segmentation; ChatGPT for VQA answer parsing and evaluation
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Object hallucination in LVLMs can lead to unexpected consequences in real-world applications. For example, an autonomous driving system with incorrect understanding of the external environment could make wrong decisions when encountering unexpected events, potentially leading to serious safety issues. The work aims to improve reliability and safety of LVLMs in deployment.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Visual instruction datasets used to train LVLMs (mostly based on MSCOCO) have an unbalanced object distribution where top frequent objects occupy a major part. This causes LVLMs to be prone to hallucinate frequently appearing objects and objects that frequently co-occur with ground-truth objects. Approximately half of hallucinated objects in each image belong to the top 10 frequently appearing COCO objects.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The evaluation focuses only on coarse-grained object hallucination (object level), not fine-grained aspects such as object number, attributes, or positions. Evaluation is conducted on a subset of the validation set due to computational resource limitations, which may be affected by data distribution. POPE uses a matching-based method to determine Yes/No answers, but LVLMs may occasionally fail to provide explicit Yes/No answers, leading to inaccurate results. When using automatic segmentation tools, object labels may be inconsistent with human annotations. Only a small number of LVLMs are evaluated, excluding recently released or closed-source models.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing and evaluation of object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). The dataset supports evaluation under three difficulty settings (Random, Popular, Adversarial) and can be extended to unannotated datasets using automatic segmentation tools. It can also be used to analyze the impact of hallucination on downstream vision tasks such as VQA and image captioning.
